{"id": "79678321-594e-4ec0-bc3b-3c5b463a0c2f", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_ejr1QSeUuVLDLZxLALUOLz", "content": "[{'text': '## Documentation search results\\n\\n{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"ADVCOST05-BP06 Use provisioned throughput for steady-state agents and on-demand pricing for variable workloads\",\"context\":\"## Implementation guidance\\\\n\\\\nAmazon Bedrock has three pricing models for inference: on-demand\\\\n(pay per token with no commitment), Provisioned Throughput\\\\n(reserved capacity at a lower per-token rate with time-based\\\\ncommitment), and batch inference (lowest per-token rate for\\\\nasynchronous, latency-tolerant workloads). If you pick the wrong\\\\nmodel for an agent\\'s pattern, you risk overpaying either through\\\\nidle reserved capacity or through premium on-demand rates on\\\\nsteady-state volume.\\\\n\\\\nThe break-even calculation for Provisioned Throughput compares the\\\\ncommitted hourly rate against what the same invocation volume\\\\nwould cost on-demand. Agents with consistent, predictable volume\\\\nthat exceeds this threshold (brand safety monitors running around\\\\nthe clock and constant content classification) benefit from\\\\nProvisioned Throughput. Agents with spiky, unpredictable patterns\\\\n(campaign planning that surges during launch cycles and seasonal\\\\ncreative generation) typically cost less on-demand because the\\\\nidle hours during low-demand periods would waste reserved\\\\ncapacity. Provisioned Throughput is available with no commitment\\\\n(hourly), 1-month, or 6-month terms. Teams can start with the\\\\nno-commitment option to validate utilization before locking into\\\\nterm discounts.\\\\n\\\\nBatch eligibility depends on whether a workload can be deferred.\\\\nIf an inference consumer reads the result hours after it is\\\\nproduced, it is paying for an unused low-latency guarantee.\\\\nAmazon Bedrock batch inference prices that difference by queuing\\\\nrequests and processing them when capacity is available, at lower\\\\nper-token rates.\\\\n\\\\nThe completion window for batch inference is a range, not a\\\\nguaranteed deadline. A downstream consumer that assumes a fixed\\\\ncompletion time treats an occasional slow batch as a missing-data\\\\nincident. Batch jobs can\\'t support conversational or tool-calling\\\\ninteractions, so a workflow that mixes deferrable analysis with\\\\ninteractive steps must be split at that boundary.\\\\n\\\\nAction group functions on\\\\nAWS Lambda are a separate cost that compounds with inference\\\\ncosts. Each agent invocation might trigger multiple Lambda calls\\\\nfor tool use (such as database lookups, API calls, and\\\\ncalculations). Lambda charges for both invocation count and\\\\nduration multiplied by allocated memory. Over-provisioned memory\\\\nincreases cost without reducing execution time when the function\\\\nis I/O-bound rather than compute-bound.\\\\nAWS Lambda Power Tuning tests memory configurations to find the\\\\npoint where additional memory stops improving performance, the\\\\nminimum cost\\\\n\\\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/video-streaming-advertising-lens/advcost05-bp06.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Effective cost optimization strategies for Amazon Bedrock | Artificial Intelligence\",\"context\":\"### Use batch inference\\\\n\\\\nWith batch mode, you can get simultaneous large-scale predictions by providing a set of prompts as a single input file and receiving responses as a single output file. The responses are processed and stored in your Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket so you can access them later. Amazon Bedrock offers select FMs from leading AI providers like Anthropic, Meta, Mistral AI, and Amazon for batch inference at a 50% lower price compared to On-Demand inference pricing. Refer to Supported AWS Regions and models for batch inference for more details. This approach is ideal for non-real-time workloads where you need to process large volumes of content efficiently.\\\\n\\\\n**Best practice:** Identify workloads in your application that don\u2019t require real-time responses and migrate them to batch processing. For example, instead of generating product descriptions on-demand when users view them, pre-generate descriptions for new products in a nightly batch job and store the results. This approach can dramatically reduce your FM costs while maintaining the same output quality\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/effective-cost-optimization-strategies-for-amazon-bedrock/\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"How to estimate Amazon Bedrock costs for public sector applications | AWS Public Sector Blog\",\"context\":\"### Inference\\\\n\\\\nWhen you submit an input to an FM, the model predicts a probable sequence of tokens and returns that sequence as the output. This is known as inference. Amazon Bedrock provides you the capability of running inference with the FM of your choice. Therefore, model inference is the primary driver for costs incurred with Amazon Bedrock. There are different options available for inference, and pricing can vary across these different types:\\\\n\\\\n* **On-Demand** \u2013 With this option, you get maximum flexibility since you only pay for what you use, without any long-term commitments. When using text models, you\u2019re charged based on the tokens processed \u2013 both for input and output. For embedding models, you just pay for input tokens processed. If you\u2019re generating images, the charge is per image.\\\\n* **Batch processing** \u2013 In batch processing, you submit multiple requests in a single input file and get all responses in one output file. These results are stored in your Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket for easy access later. Batch mode costs 50 percent less than On-Demand mode for select AI models from providers like Anthropic, Meta, Mistral AI, and Amazon.\\\\n* **Provisioned Throughput** \u2013 With Provisioned Throughput allows you to purchase dedicated model units for your specific base or custom models where you get throughput when you need it most. Each model unit purchased provides a specific throughput capacity, measured by the maximum number of tokens (both input and output) that can be processed per minute. The pricing follows an hourly charging model with added discounts for commitments.\\\\n* **Prompt caching** \u2013 Prompt caching in Amazon Bedrock adds portions of your context to a cache. The model can use the cache to skip recomputation of inputs and reduce input token processing cost as well as latency. When using prompt caching, you\u2019re charged at a reduced rate for tokens read from cache. Depending on the model, however, tokens written to cache might be charged at a rate that is higher than that of uncached input tokens.\\\\n* **Latency-optimized inference** \u2013Latency-optimized inference in Amazon Bedrock delivers significantly faster response times for FM without compromising accuracy. Developers can set the \u201cLatency\u201d parameter to \u201coptimized\u201d in the Amazon Bedrock runtime API to access this capability. For pricing details, check each model\u2019s pricing for latency-optimized inference\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/publicsector/how-to-estimate-amazon-bedrock-costs-for-public-sector-applications/\"},{\"rank_order\":4,\"title\":\"Amazon Bedrock\",\"context\":\"### Pricing model\\\\n\\\\nAmazon Bedrock offers flexible pricing based on API consumption. Organizations pay for input and output tokens processed during on-demand usage, or they can use and scale imported FMs measured in capacity units.\\\\n\\\\nBedrock exposes four inference service tiers \u2014 **Reserved**, **Priority**, **Standard**, and **Flex** \u2014 that let a workload trade off availability, latency, and cost without changing models or APIs. Three of them (Priority, Standard, Flex) are on-demand and share a single per-model quota; tier selection is just a request-time parameter. The fourth (Reserved) is a separate pool with its own SLA and minimum commitment. This sits alongside Bedrock\\'s other capacity controls \u2014 Provisioned Throughput for custom and imported models, batch inference, and cross-region inference \u2014 and is usually the first lever to reach for on shared on-demand models\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/gen-ai-inference-architecture-and-best-practices-on-aws/amazon-bedrock.html\"},{\"rank_order\":5,\"title\":\"Automate Amazon Bedrock batch inference: Building a scalable and efficient pipeline | Artificial Intelligence\",\"context\":\"## Artificial Intelligence\\\\n\\\\n# Automate Amazon Bedrock batch inference: Building a scalable and efficient pipeline\\\\n\\\\nAmazon Bedrock is a fully managed service that offers a choice of high-performing foundation models (FMs) from leading AI companies such as AI21 Labs, Anthropic, Cohere, Meta, Mistral AI, Stability AI, and Amazon through a single API, along with a broad set of capabilities you need to build generative AI applications with security, privacy, and responsible AI.\\\\n\\\\nBatch inference in Amazon Bedrock efficiently processes large volumes of data using foundation models (FMs) when real-time results aren\u2019t necessary. It\u2019s ideal for workloads that aren\u2019t latency sensitive, such as obtaining embeddings, entity extraction, FM-as-judge evaluations, and text categorization and summarization for business reporting tasks. A key advantage is its cost-effectiveness, with batch inference workloads charged at a 50% discount compared to On-Demand pricing. Refer to Supported Regions and models for batch inference for current supporting AWS Regions and models.\\\\n\\\\nAlthough batch inference offers numerous benefits, it\u2019s limited to 10 batch inference jobs submitted per model per Region. To address this consideration and enhance your use of batch inference, we\u2019ve developed a scalable solution using AWS Lambda and Amazon DynamoDB. This post guides you through implementing a queue management system that automatically monitors available job slots and submits new jobs as slots become available.\\\\n\\\\nWe walk you through our solution, detailing the core logic of the Lambda functions. By the end, you\u2019ll understand how to implement this solution so you can maximize the efficiency of your batch inference workflows on Amazon Bedrock. For instructions on how to start your Amazon Bedrock batch inference job, refer to Enhance call center efficiency using batch inference for transcript summarization with Amazon Bedrock\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/automate-amazon-bedrock-batch-inference-building-a-scalable-and-efficient-pipeline/\"}]}}\\n\\n## Recent AWS announcements (What\\'s New)\\n\\nNewer than your training data may be. When these conflict with the documentation results above or with what you remember, prefer the most recent dated source.\\n\\n{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"What\\'s New at AWS - Cloud Innovation & News\",\"context\":\"Amazon Bedrock, a service offered by AWS, has expanded its support for Batch inference for two new models: Anthropic\\'s Claude Sonnet 4 and OpenAI\\'s GPT-OSS 120B and 20B. With Batch inference, users can process multiple inference requests concurrently, improving performance and reducing costs by up to 50% compared to on-demand inference pricing\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2025/08/amazon-bedrock-batch-inference-anthropic-claude-sonnet-4-openai-gpt-oss-models/\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Amazon Bedrock introduces Priority and Flex inference service tiers - AWS\",\"context\":\"Amazon Bedrock, a service offered by AWS, has introduced two new inference service tiers: Flex and Priority. The Flex tier is designed for non-interactive workloads that can tolerate longer latencies, making it suitable for model evaluations, content summarization, labeling and annotation, and multistep agentic workflow. These new service tiers are available for leading foundation models like OpenAI (gpt-oss-20b, gpt-oss-120b), DeepSeek (DeepSeek V3.1), Qwen3 (Coder-480B-A35B-Instruct, Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct, 32B dense, Qwen3-235B-A22B-2507), and Amazon Nova (Nova Pro and Nova Premier). {"id": "ace708f7-12ff-4c2b-b0c8-474376078fd5", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Yes. An overnight report that nobody waits for is a good fit for Bedrock's cheaper asynchronous options. The documentation backs this up, but I haven't seen your actual usage or model.

**Options, from biggest saving to smallest**

1. **Batch inference** gives the biggest saving. For supported models, it costs about 50% less than on-demand per token. You put your prompts in one file in S3 and Bedrock writes the results to S3 as a single output file. It was built for work like report generation, summarization, and classification.
   - **Model support:** Batch inference only works for select models and Regions. That includes some Anthropic, Meta, Mistral, and Amazon models. Check that yours is one of them.
   - **Timing:** The completion window is a range, not a deadline. The report should leave a buffer before whoever reads it needs it.
   - **Job limit:** The default is 10 batch jobs per model per Region. If you need more, queue them.
   - **Interactive steps:** Batch can't do conversational or tool-calling interactions. If the report mixes those with plain generation, split the pipeline there. Batch the generation steps and keep the interactive steps on-demand.

2. **The Flex service tier** is the fallback if your model doesn't support batch. You choose it per request with a parameter, so there's no pipeline change. It costs less than Standard but gets lower priority when demand is high. The launch list included OpenAI gpt-oss, DeepSeek V3.1, Qwen3, and Amazon Nova Pro and Premier. Check whether your model has been added since.

3. **Prompt caching** works with either option. If every report request repeats a large shared prompt or context, cached input tokens are billed at a reduced rate.

**What I found in your account:** There are no batch inference jobs in us-east-1, so this workload is probably running on-demand. I didn't check other Regions or accounts.

If you tell me which model and Region the report uses, I can check whether it supports batch or Flex. I can also pull the last few weeks of Bedrock usage to estimate the saving. If the report really is half your spend, batch would cut that half by about 50% and the total bill by about 25%.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
